extracted.intended_audience: Congressional committee members, Department of the Interior officials, Bureau of Indian Affairs staff, tribal leaders and tribal legal advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed statutory/administrative criteria and procedures for determining federal acknowledgment (recognition) of Indian tribes, including evidentiary factors, burdens of proof, and limits on Department of the Interior discretion. Intended to shape how S.2375 and BIA regulations determine tribal status and access to federal Indian services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'Indian Tribe' by series of definitional factors
rubrics_metrics.description: "THE TERM 'INDIAN TRIBE' IS DEFINED BY ANY OF A SERIES OF DEFINITIONAL FACTORS ENUMERATED W[m] RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH FOLLOW, AND IS INTENDED TO APPLY TO ALL INDIAN PEOPLE, INCLUDING INDIAN COMMUNITIES, BANDS, SOCIETIES, ALLIANCES AND GROUPS..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission's definition is explicitly multi-factor and inclusive — intended to apply broadly to Indian peoples (communities, bands, societies, alliances and groups) and not to divide or retroactively alter the status of already federally-recognized tribal entities. Use the enumerated factors (below) rather than a single rigid test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision authority: Department of the Interior (not 'United States')
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendment replaces the term 'Federal Government' or 'United States' with the 'Department of the Interior' in statutes governing acknowledgment decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill should clarify that the Department of the Interior (and its delegated office) is the entity that administers acknowledgment decisions and procedures; statutory language should reflect that focus rather than implying all federal agencies share identical acknowledgement responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an administrative procedure and policy guidelines for acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative procedure and policy guidelines are to be established and followed by the Department of the Interior in its decision to acknowledge the existence of certain Indian tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The acknowledgment process must be a defined administrative procedure with published guidelines so petitioning groups understand standards, evidence types, process, and reviewability. The acknowledgment should be premised on establishment of a government-to-government relationship with federally acknowledged tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify scope: Act deals with services provided by the Department of the Interior
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend title and text to make clear the legislation is intended to deal with services provided by the Department of the Interior to groups so acknowledged, not services provided by other Federal agencies such as HEW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit or specify statutory scope to avoid confusion about which agency's programs/benefits are implicated; cross-agency consequences should be addressed explicitly in separate provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of DOI acknowledgment not to render group ineligible for other agency services
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert new paragraph (2)(a)(5): 'The failure of any petitioning tribal group to have its existence acknowledged by the Department of the Interior pursuant to the provisions of this Act, should not be construed by any other federal agency or department as ineligibility for special Indian services or benefits provided otherwise qualified groups by such agency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect petitioning groups from automatic denial of services by other federal agencies solely because DOI has not acknowledged them under this Act. Agencies should retain independent eligibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and reviewability of Secretary's evidentiary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed language: 'provided, however, the decision of the Secretary to include any evidence offered by the Department of the Interior, or to exclude any evidence offered by a petitioning tribal group, shall be reviewable as provided in this Act with the burden of proof being on the United States to establish the relevancy or irrelevancy of any evidence so included or so excluded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Secretary's decisions to admit or exclude evidence in the acknowledgment proceeding should be subject to judicial review and the United States should bear the burden of proving that evidence is relevant or irrelevant when contested. This limits unfettered discretion and helps remedy historic Departmental practices that could disadvantage petitioning groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary lacks lawmaking authority; decisions subject to judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to add a proviso clarifying that the Secretary 'does not have lawmaking authority and that this IS subject to judicial review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirm that the Secretary's factual and evidentiary determinations are administrative, not legislative, and may be reviewed by courts to ensure fairness and legal sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable evidence of longstanding tribal political authority and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewritten factor: 'The group exhibits evidence of a longstanding tribal political authority or other influence over the members of the group or possesses a longstanding relationship with the United States or particular States based upon a government's acknowledgment of the Indian group's separate or distinct status.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be demonstrated by showing the group has had a tribal council or other structure or method used as its own form of government or as a means of making group decisions or to determine its membership; furthermore, such evidence shall include traditional social mechanisms or political structures or organizations unique to the group. Do not require formal U.S.-style governmental institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require formal U.S.-modeled governmental structure (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of BIA practice: prior Bureau requirements forced groups to have a formal governmental structure 'patterned after that of the United States' to qualify; this is said to be unfair and effectively requires prior federal recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition criteria should allow indigenous forms of governance and social organization; courts and statutes should not demand U.S.-style institutions as a prerequisite for acknowledgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: Prior treaty or formal relations with U.S./States as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed new 5(b)(1): 'the group has had treaty relations with the United States or particular States, or preexisting colonial or territorial governments. "Treaty relations" shall include any formal relationship based on a government acknowledgement of the Indian group's separate or distinct status.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfaction of a history of treaty relations or other formal governmental relationships should be treated as prima facie evidence of entitlement to federal acknowledgment — sufficient (by itself) to establish acknowledgment in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor: Prior identification by Act of Congress or Executive order as prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed new 5(b)(2): 'the group has been identified or referred to as an Indian tribe or designated as Indian by an Act of Congress or Executive order which may have provided for, specified or identified the rights, governmental structures, jurisdiction, or property of the tribal group.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic congressional or executive recognition that defined or assigned rights, jurisdiction, governmental structures, or property to the group should serve as prima facie evidence for federal acknowledgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of factors 6 and 7 as immediately prima facie evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal: move factors 6 and 7 into a new section so that 'Notwithstanding any of the above factors, satisfaction of either of the two factors immediately below shall be prima facie evidence of entitlement to Federal acknowledgment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where present, these powerful historical indicators (e.g., treaty relations or prior official identification) should automatically establish entitlement absent very strong contrary justification; this prevents technicalities from denying long-established claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique/possible deletion of identification-by-others factor (Sec.5(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation from regional conference: Section 5(c)(1) calling for identification of Indians by governmental authorities, public documents or scholars over a protracted period should be deleted because (1) legitimate tribal groups may have been continually ignored by non-Indian media/authorities; (2) such identification is not necessarily knowledgeable or informed; (3) identification by other acknowledged Indian groups is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on historical external identification (by non-Indians) as a gating criterion; consider peer-identification by other indigenous groups and the group's own historical continuity instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend notices and findings to be adverse-to-petitioning-group cognizant
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendment to Sec.6(a): insert phrase 'adverse to the petitioning group' after 'decision' so that the Department's decision-making and notifications reference adverse actions clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure procedural fairness and notice when the Department issues decisions unfavorable to petitioning groups; administrative language should explicitly account for adverse findings and associated rights (e.g., to respond or seek review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a 'catch-22' by requiring formal structures that could only exist if previously recognized
rubrics_metrics.description: Text argues the original bill's criteria would require a group to have been previously 'federally recognized' (or have had a U.S.-style government) in order to meet criteria — creating an impossible loop for unacknowledged groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition rules should be written to avoid circularity: do not require evidence that presupposes prior federal recognition. Allow alternative forms of evidence (tradition, social mechanisms, historical relations) to demonstrate tribal existence and authority.
